title: All Souls (2 November)
hookLine: November is the month of the dead; graves visited and names read
tomorrow: The Dedication of the Lateran (9 November)

cards: In the first days of November, the cemeteries of Poland glow after dark.

Small candles in red and white glass jars flicker on grave after grave, the well-known and the forgotten, until a whole hillside looks like a field of embers. In Mexico, families sit at graves with marigolds and food.
In a parish church in Ohio, a priest stands at the ambo and reads aloud, one by one, the names of everyone from the parish who died in the past year.

teach.b: Yesterday was for all the saints in heaven. Today is for all the faithful departed: everyone who has died, and especially those who, Catholics believe, are still being made ready for God.

The Church calls that purification purgatory. It isn't a second chance or a halfway hell; it's understood as the last stretch of being healed, and Catholics believe the living can help with their prayers.
One scripture the Church points to is in the second book of Maccabees, which is in the Catholic Bible.

After a battle, Judas Maccabeus takes up a collection so that sacrifice can be offered for the fallen, and the text says, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead."

Catholics and Orthodox Christians pray for the dead; many Protestant churches do not, and Protestant Bibles leave Maccabees out or set it apart with the Apocrypha. As a single day, All Souls comes from a monastery.

teach.h: ODILO OF CLUNY: A DAY FOR ALL.
teach.b: Odilo, abbot of the great monastery of Cluny in France, ordered his monks to pray for all the dead on the day after All Saints, and the custom spread.
During the First World War, with so many dying, Pope Benedict XV allowed every priest to celebrate three Masses on this day.

teach.h: A HOLY AND WHOLESOME THOUGHT TO PRAY FOR THE DEAD.
teach.b: The old Latin prayer for the dead, still said at funerals and graves, is short: "Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine." Eternal rest give unto them, O Lord. That's where the word requiem comes from.
And week ninety-eight closes: Mary's birthday, the cross lifted high, the mother who stood, Francis, the rosary, all the saints, and now all the dead.

how: On All Souls Day, 2 November, Catholics pray for the dead, attend Mass, and visit and decorate graves; through November many parishes keep a book of names of the dead near the altar and read aloud the names of parishioners who died that year.

games.q: you're Judas Maccabeus after a battle. some of your fallen soldiers were found carrying tokens from idols. what do you do?
o: take up a collection so sacrifice can be offered for them.
strike their names from the record.
games.why: he sends the collection to Jerusalem for a sacrifice for the dead. the text calls it a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead.

practice: Stand at a grave you know, if there's a cemetery near you, or sit and bring one person who has died to mind. Say their full name, out loud if you can, and remember one specific thing: a voice, a phrase, a smell.
If you pray, say the old line, eternal rest give unto them, O Lord; if you don't, simply remember.

wordCard.voice: All Souls. The second of November, when Catholics pray for all the faithful departed, and the beginning of the month of the dead. Today's word.
